title: Ancestor Bodhidharma
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Bodhidharma, beginning with his meeting with Emperor Wu in Case 1 of the Blue Cliff Record, where the answers are "Empty, no holiness" and "I don't know." Kanho opens with grief over the war in Ukraine on Easter morning, then moves to the legends of nine years of wall sitting, including the eyelids that become tea plants. Kanho reads from the Outline of Practice and its four practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing, and practicing the Dharma. The koan of skin, flesh, bones, and marrow follows, with Dogen's reading that each student's answer expresses the Dharma fully. The story ends with Bodhidharma's tomb, opened to reveal a single sandal.

sentences.text: Happy Easter, my good friends.
I hope you're all well and that your life is good.
The sun is shining outside.
It's getting a little bit warmer in the Pacific Northwest.
Many, many kids are outside right now trying to find their Easter eggs.
Could it be more perfect?
And yet, and yet, today is Easter.
Everything is beautiful.
And I was crying so hard during Zazen because I've been seeing the pictures from the Ukraine of the suffering there.
You go and ask Ukrainian kids right now how they like Easter.
It's not about the kids being happy and liking Easter, but the untold suffering that is imposed on these people right now.
This very moment, people are in hospitals and hospitals are apparently being targeted.
And of course, my national karma kicks in.
I do remember that before I was born, it was Germany who imposed similar suffering on other people.
It was as much cause as the Russians have right now to invade: distraction from interior collapse, distraction from weakness of the people in power.
And of course, the Russian leadership is reaping the wartime benefit of their actions.
Eighty percent of the people polled in Russia really support Vladimir Putin and his war.
Of course, we cannot forget the propaganda that has been spread on their media.
We cannot forget how in the U.S. people were just willing to support someone who was setting himself up as a dictator.
So I don't know what to say other than that my heart is breaking.
And it shows us that how we feel, what we think, is a result of causes and conditions.
Our causes and conditions are that we're sitting in the sun, that it's Easter, that kids are running around outside looking for Easter eggs.
I don't want to deny them their joy, but it's causes and conditions that make us go, "Oh, such a nice day."
So I'm sorry that I started with this downer.
And it is what's real.
It is what is happening.
So, on to the official Dharma talk.
It's interesting.
I started to write about the Mountains and Water Sutra.
It is a beautiful fascicle by Ehe Dogen.
It is wonderful.

There are so many phrases and turns, and it's so elegant, and it just totally did not connect with me when I was writing, because pictures of war and suffering just kept on popping up, and the imagery of the Mountains and Water Sutra.
I couldn't match them up.
I really want to be honest and right from the heart.
So somehow we are ending up with a talk about Bodhidharma.
If we look at our Indian ancestors, their words and imagery are very flowery, and gold parasols and white elephants and true mountains pop up all over the place in the Mahayana Sutras.
But Dogen just delivers a different message.
Or maybe it would be much better to say he delivers the message differently.
I don't know if we have any relative newcomers here.
Nope.
All old hands at the Zen language and our service and so on.

But I remember when I started practicing, the first time I went to the Bellingham Zen practice group and I experienced service, I was just going, what the hey, did I just chant "Avalokiteshvara, Shariputra, Manjushri, Mahaprajnaparamita, Bodhidharma"?
Who are these people?
The list of foreign-sounding names is quite long.
So I was scratching my head quite a bit during service.
Then I found myself a Buddhist dictionary and started to look up some of these names.
One of those names, Bodhidharma, is who we will talk about today.
And he shows up in koans too.
We know by now that some people describe koans as puzzles without a solution, mind benders that push the mind to a point of giving up on a conceptual response, et cetera.
We usually say that koans are family stories of our Zen ancestors.
And Zen ancestor is definitely what Bodhidharma is.
Millions of people come from lineages that started with him.
I'll talk about his history, and a couple of koans where he is mentioned.
He was the 28th of our ancestors.
When we chant the lineage of Zen ancestors, he's number 28.
And we chant during the echo that he was our first ancestor in China.
I will also briefly touch, well, maybe not so briefly, it got bigger and bigger, on his most well-known teaching, which is called the Outline of Practice.

I'm pretty sure you've heard these lines before: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not founded upon words and letters, pointing directly to the human mind, seeing into one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.
So yes, that was Bodhidharma.
Talking about his life and the history of the time, his birthplace, and so on, I will sound like there is great certainty.
Not so, my friends, not so.
There are scholars who are equally sure that this historical Bodhidharma never existed.
However, I'm going with version one.
I like it.
I will leave it up to you to decide for yourself.
Writing this talk, I heavily leaned on Red Pine's book of the same title, Bodhidharma.
It's quite a nice book.
It shows us the Chinese and the English together.
This very famous, classical, maybe, Outline of Practice is only three of these pages long, and I was so tempted to read all of it.
But I also had to leave out many theories or alternative timelines to keep the talk somewhat coherent.
So the story goes that Bodhidharma was born around the year 440 in Kanchi, the capital of the southern kingdom of Palawa.
Others say it was the Tamil region.
Bodhidharma was the third son of a king, and he was born a Brahmin.
When he was young, he converted to Buddhism, apparently with the support of his father, because his father invited Prajna Tara, who taught him the Dharma.
Prajna Tara is our 27th ancestor.
So from warm hand to warm hand, the Dharma was transmitted.
Prajna Tara asked his student to go to China.
Often I hear it said that Bodhidharma brought Buddhism to China, which simply is not true.
However, he founded the lineage of Zen ancestors in China.
So maybe he did bring Buddhism to China.
However, when he arrived, there were, I rounded these numbers down quite a bit, more than 8,000 temples already and more than 110,000 clergy.
Fifty years later, there were about 2 million clergy and the number of temples had also exploded.
Not due to Bodhidharma, because he remained relatively unknown for the next couple of centuries.
One more item of history: at the time, China was divided into Northern China and Southern China.
Shortly after Bodhidharma's death, Northern China was divided into East and West China.
In Southern China, Buddhism was mostly confined to the educated elite.
But in the North, Buddhism was quickly spreading through the general population.
Bodhidharma arrived in Southern China probably somewhere around 475.
And now to the first koan.
This is where the famous encounter with Emperor Wu happened.
This story is famous to this day.
In the most popular koan collection, the Blue Cliff Record, it is koan number one.
In our Zen version of a koan collection, in our Soto collection, the Book of Serenity, it is koan number two.
Let me read it to you.
*Case one of the Blue Cliff Record.
Emperor Wu of Liang asked the great master Bodhidharma, "What is the highest meaning of the holy truth?"
Bodhidharma said, "Empty, no holiness."*
Let me insert something here.
I must have really stunned this emperor.
He has this famous person of Buddhism in front of him, and he's not getting the answers he was looking for.
In other versions, it's also said that the emperor asked Bodhidharma, "I've built many temples, and what is my merit?"
And Bodhidharma said, "No merit."
*So the emperor said, "Who is facing me?"
Bodhidharma replied, "I don't know."
The emperor did not understand.*
*After this, Bodhidharma crossed the Yangtze River and came to the Kingdom of Wei.* That's in northern China.
*Later, the emperor brought this up to his minister, Master Chi, and asked him about it.
Master Chi asked, "Does your majesty know who this man is?"
The emperor said, "I don't know."
Master Chi said, "He is the Maha-sattva Avalokiteshvara transmitting the Buddha mind seal."
The emperor felt regretful.
So he wanted to send an emissary to go invite Bodhidharma to return.
Master Chi told him, "Your majesty, don't say that you will send someone to fetch him back.
Even if everyone in the whole country were to go after him, he still would not return."*
So Bodhidharma traveled for a few years and he finally settled in northern China at Shaolin Temple.
In Dogen's Fukanzazengi [unclear: "Bichang"]:
*Need I mention the Buddha who was possessed of inborn knowledge?
The influence of his six years of upright sitting is noticeable still.
Or Bodhidharma's transmission of the mind seal, the fame of his nine years of wall sitting is celebrated to this day.
Since this was the case with the saints of old, how can we today dispense with negotiation of the way?*
Yes, it is said that Bodhidharma sat in his cave for nine years, and among the locals, he was apparently known as the Indian who stares at a wall.
To the Chinese, he must have looked very foreign with his blue eyes.
And in some koans, there's a reference that he had a red beard.
More about those seven years: there's a story that in his seventh year, Bodhidharma fell asleep while meditating.
So he cut off his eyelids, and where he dropped his eyelids, tea plants sprouted to keep practitioners awake forever after.
It is also said that he sat for so long that his buttocks rotted away.
That is often when you see the little Bodhidharma figurines, the red ones with big bulbous eyes, no eyelids.
It's usually rather roundish and no legs, but I don't think he really lost his legs.
So I don't know what he found in those nine years, but it must have been something that he transmitted to the next generation of Buddha ancestors.
He also became well known locally.
Now, if you ever run across Shaolin monastery, like in the movies, I'm almost sure it wasn't about Zen history.
More likely, it would be a Kung Fu flick.
To this day, Shaolin temple is famous for its martial arts training, which, by the way, does continue to this day.
Legends describe that Bodhidharma was disturbed by the poor physical and mental shape of the Shaolin monks.
So he taught them techniques to improve their physical condition, and he taught them meditation.
He is said to have taught a series of external exercises called the 18 arhat hands.
Arhat is similar to Bodhisattva.
And an internal practice called the sinew metamorphosis classic.
In addition, after his departure from the temple, two of Bodhidharma's manuscripts were said to be discovered inside the temple.
Copies of one of the documents still exist today.
So Bodhidharma's teachings were recorded and they were written down.
Copies of his teaching from the 7th century were discovered in 1900 in the Tanhuang caves.
His best-known sermon is the Outline of Practice that I mentioned before.
It is amazingly brief and terse, quite a step away from the flowery language of the Avatamsaka and Vimalakirti sutras.
It's just a little bit too long for me to read all of it to you.
But if you look for it on the internet, you can find it.
If you can't find it and you're interested, please send me an email and I'll send you a link.
It's definitely worth reading and studying deeply.
So today I can only give you a taste of it, and I have to leave out quite a bit.
The blue-eyed barbarian, this is what he said.
*Many roads lead to the path, but basically there are only two, reason and practice.

To enter by reason means to realize the essence through instruction and to believe that all living things share the same true nature, which isn't apparent because it's shrouded by sensation and delusion.

Those who turn from delusion back to reality, who meditate on walls, the absence of self and other, the oneness of mortal and sage, and to remain unmoved, even by scriptures, are in complete and unspoken agreement with reason.
Without moving, without effort, they enter, we say, by reason.*

*To enter by practice refers to four all-inclusive practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing and practicing the Dharma.* Let me repeat that, because that's like core practice.
*To enter by practice refers to four all-inclusive practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing and practicing the Dharma.*
I skipped suffering injustice.
He just shows karmic relation, past and future.
That's the one we all know, how to suffer injustice, right?
Or how to feel it, how to cope with it.
That's what he describes.
But I'm going to go on to adapting to conditions.
*As mortals, we are ruled by conditions, not by ourselves.
All the suffering and joy we experience depend on conditions.
If we should be blessed by some great reward, such as fame or fortune, it's the fruit of a seed planted by us in the past.* Now, this is important.
*When conditions change, it ends.* When conditions change, it ends.
*Why delight in its existence?
But while success and failure depend on conditions, the mind neither waxes nor wanes.
Those who remain unmoved by the wind of joy silently follow the path.*
*Third, seeking nothing.
People of this world are deluded.
They are always longing for something, always, in a word, seeking.
But the wise wake up.
They choose reason over custom.
They fix their mind on the sublime and let their bodies change with the seasons.
All phenomena are empty.
They contain nothing worth desiring.
Calamity forever alternates with prosperity.
To dwell in the three realms is to dwell in a burning house.
To have a body is to suffer.
Does anybody with a body know peace?
Those who understand this detach themselves from all that exists and stop imagining or seeking anything.
The sutras say, to seek is to suffer.
To seek nothing is bliss.* And that's the last of the four core practices.
*When you seek nothing, you are on the path.*
*Fourth, practicing the Dharma.
The Dharma is the truth that all natures are pure.* Let me repeat that.
*When you seek nothing, you are on the path.* Practicing the Dharma.
*The Dharma is the truth that all natures are pure.
By this truth, all appearances are empty.
Defilement and attachment, subject and object, do not exist.
Those wise enough to believe and understand these truths are bound to practice according to the Dharma.

And since that which is real includes nothing worth begrudging, they give their body, life, and property in charity without regret, without the vanity of giver, gift, or recipient, and without bias or attachment.
Thus, through their own practice, they are able to help others and glorify the way of enlightenment.
And as with charity, they also practice the other virtues.*
He's referring to the paramitas here.
*But while practicing the six virtues to eliminate delusion, they practice nothing at all.
That is what's meant by practicing the Dharma.*
I really think this is one of the greatest sermons in our tradition.
In three brief pages, Bodhidharma outlined our practice, our belief that everything is Buddha nature, the teaching of non-separation, the Four Noble Truths, the paramitas.
He was able to put it all in three short pages.
There are many more stories of Bodhidharma and his students, how Weike came to Bodhidharma asking for the teaching, and Bodhidharma just kept on refusing him.
It is said that Weike cut off his arm to demonstrate his sincerity.
Please don't do that.
Bodhidharma had some well-known students, and they show up in this koan.
Bodhidharma decided that it was time to transmit the Dharma, and he asked his four students to come forth and demonstrate their understanding.
Here comes the koan.
*Bodhidharma asked, "Can each of you say something to demonstrate your understanding?"
Tao Fu stepped forward and said, "It is not bound by words and phrases, nor is it separate from words and phrases.
This is the function of the Tao."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my skin."
The nun Songzhe stepped up and said, "It is like a glorious glimpse of the realm of Akshobhya Buddha.
Seen once, it need not be seen again."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my flesh."
Tao Yu said, "The four elements are all empty.
The five skandhas are without actual existence.
Not a single dharma can be grasped."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my bones."
Finally, Weike came forth, bowed deeply in silence, and stood up straight.
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my marrow."*
Bodhidharma passed on the symbolic robe and bowl of Dharma succession to Weike and, some texts claim, a copy of the Lankavatara Sutra.
The standard reading of this koan in certain literature is usually that Weike got it and the others didn't.
That's why he received the bowl and the robe.
Dogen, however, God, I love Dogen, he came up with a different understanding.
In Dogen's understanding, Weike was not the winner of the contest, and the others were not losers, nor was their understanding somehow lesser.
Dogen said that that understanding was not correct.
Every expression of Dharma is a true and full expression of Dharma, and every expression is different.
Then each one of these statements is true and full.
We all take our Dharma position, whatever and wherever it happens to be, and there is nothing lacking.
So there was no hierarchy.
I want to see how someone without a skin would live, or someone without bones and without flesh.
So no hierarchy of expression.
The Dharma is expressed fully according to each person's Dharma position.
Just like us right now.
You're all sitting here.
We're bringing up the Dharma together.
Priests, lay people, brief experience, long experience, brand new.
Dharma position is just where we are.
That's what it means to practice.
And even if we don't practice, we're still doing it.
So as you saw, Bodhidharma had only a few disciples, and his was the first teaching of what was called the Jhana school in India.
When it came to China and from there to Korea and later to Japan, the teaching flourished.
In China, the Jhana school became Chan.
In Japan, it became Zen.
We have a wonderful book that describes the life of the first ancestors.
It was written two Dharma generations after Dogen.
It's called Transmission of Light.
There are other versions called the Transmission of the Lamp.
They describe the lives of different Dharma teachers.
And I just saw that I made a mistake before when I wrote the talk.
I said that Bodhidharma was the 28th.
He's the 29th.
Sorry, I must have skipped one.
Prajna Tara was the 28th.
So Jhana became Zen in Japan.
The Jhana school flowered in China, in Korea, and in Japan.
In the Transmission of Light, this book here, it describes some of the struggles that Bodhidharma had.
Two local precept masters apparently really hated him.
It is written that they tried to poison him several times.
They threw rocks at him, and they knocked out his front teeth.
So Bodhidharma decided it was time to go home after he transmitted the Dharma to his students.
One version says he actually died immediately after he transmitted the Dharma and didn't plan on going home.
Another version provides different information about Bodhidharma's death.
Bodhidharma, he writes, died on the banks of the Luo River, and he was buried by his disciple Hui Ke, possibly in a cave.
On the other hand, a slightly different version, according to Dao Shuan's chronology: Bodhidharma's death may have occurred prior to 534, which was the date of Northern Wei's fall.
Furthermore, there's coinciding mention that the Luo River actually may have been the place of Bodhidharma's death.
It suggests that Bodhidharma died in the mass execution at Heian in 528.
Supporting this possibility is a report in the Chinese Buddhist canon stating that a Buddhist monk was among the victims at Heian.
Heian was a succession struggle between different imperial lineages.
On the other hand, about three years later, an official of one of the later Wei kingdoms claims to have encountered Bodhidharma, who told him he was returning to India.
He had a staff on his shoulder from which hung a single sandal.
And Bodhidharma, during that meeting, predicted the death of Song Yun's ruler.
When the official returned home, Song Yun had just passed away.
So they opened Bodhidharma's tomb, and all they found inside was a single sandal.
So that's Bodhidharma for us.
And this is also the end of my talk.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
